title: No punishment without law
label: ECHR Article 7 · Human Rights Act 1998
summary: No one can be convicted for an act that was not a crime when they did it. But an old law can be used in a new way.
rule: Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights, part of UK law through the Human Rights Act 1998, says no one may be held guilty of a criminal offence for an act that was not an offence when it was committed. It also forbids a heavier penalty than the one that applied at the time.
nuance: Parliament cannot create a crime after the fact. Proscription offences therefore apply only from the moment an organisation is proscribed: the 2025 order came into force on 5 July 2025, and the support offences reach expressions made from then on.

Article 7 does not stop an existing, broadly drawn law from being applied to conduct it was rarely used against before. That is the point the UK timeline makes about section 1 of the Terrorism Act 2000: the definition has been in force since 2000, so using it against protest creates no new crime. What changes is how it is used.
why_it_matters: Knowing when a law began to apply, and to what, separates conduct that was lawful at the time from conduct that was not.

history.text: The Human Rights Act 1998 gives effect to Article 7 in UK law.
The proscription order comes into force on 5 July 2025.
